1.point: Open with Musa asking Khidr to teach him, and say that the chapter will show why a guide helps and how to recognise a true one.
steps: A prophet asked a stranger to teach him (hook).
The traveller has the same need; the law set the boundary, now the question is who walks beside him.
State what the chapter will establish.

2.point: The traveller needs someone who has walked the road himself, because the soul enters states he cannot interpret alone.
steps: The soul passes into strange states that arrive without explanation.
A traveller who cannot read them can lose the way.
One who has passed through them can read them, so the guide must have travelled, not merely studied.
Conclude: a companion who has walked the road is needed.

3.point: Because the Prophet's inner knowledge passed to the Imams and not down a chain of masters, a Shia guide is a trusted adviser under the Imams, consulted for a stretch, never obeyed as a Sufi master is.
steps: Sufi orders ground a master's authority in a chain back to the Prophet.
Shia hold that inheritance went to the Imams, so no chain and no tariqa.
Hence no claim to the murid's total obedience; the Shia traveller finds a trusted person.
Tabatabaʾi names him the general teacher: consulted like anyone knowledgeable, for a stretch.
The special teachers are the Prophet and Imams, whose company is never left.
Conclude: under the Imams, not in their place.

4.point: The Shia tradition can name real teachers of this road from the last century or so, all of them outside the Sufi orders.
steps: Tabatabaʾi names his own teacher, Qadi.
Qadi's line runs back to Akhund Hamadani, who trained several guides.
These men were jurists and scholars who had nothing to do with the orders.
They taught the road this book describes (knowledge of the self).

5.point: Test a guide by whether he keeps the law, by long company, and by whether he turns people towards God; wonders and learning prove nothing.
steps: A guide must be tested; learning cannot show he has walked the road.
Wonders cannot show it either.
Keeping the law rules a false guide out.
Long company shows how far a true one has travelled.
Where company is impossible, weigh what he prescribes against Book, Sunnah and Imams.
A true guide turns people towards God, a false one towards himself.
Conclude.

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: The hook: Musa, a prophet, travels far to ask Khidr to teach him.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Draws the parallel to the traveller, recalls the law in one sentence, and states what the chapter will establish.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Supplies the premise: the soul enters unexplained states the traveller cannot read alone and may lose the way.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Supplies the inference: one who has passed through such states can read them, so the guide must have travelled rather than studied.

¶5.label: aside
¶5.why: Raises a new question, when the need begins, which the point (that a companion is needed) does not require. Bahmanpour's law-first sequence and the Sufi exaggeration are a digression; only ¶6-7's wording depends on it.

¶6.label: aside
¶6.why: The Musabbihat and Qadi's year-long instruction illustrate what a beginner needs, a sub-question the point does not use. Nothing in the section's argument would go unsupported without it.

¶7.label: restate
¶7.why: Mutahhari is a second scholar saying what ¶3-4 already established (a guide who has travelled, states the traveller cannot read alone); the Khidr couplet is glossed back to ¶3 and the last sentence states the conclusion already reached.

¶8.label: advance
¶8.why: Step one: the orders ground a master's authority in a silsila carrying the Prophet's inner knowledge.

¶9.label: advance
¶9.why: Step two: Shia hold that knowledge passed to the Imams, leaving no room for a chain; hence no tariqa.

¶10.label: advance
¶10.why: Step three: without the chain no claim to a murid's obedience; the Shia traveller finds a trusted person instead.

¶11.label: advance
¶11.why: Names the figure as Tabatabaʾi's general teacher, consulted like any knowledgeable person, and sets up the verse.

¶12.label: advance
¶12.why: Adds that the general teacher is for a stretch of the road only, and introduces the special teachers as the Prophet and Imams.

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Supplies the final step, that the Imams' inner company is never left, which is what puts the guide under them; the closing two sentences restate the point and point forward to Chapter Fifteen, and could be trimmed.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: First named teacher: Tabatabaʾi's own, Qadi, placed in living memory.

¶15.label: advance
¶15.why: Extends the line to Akhund Hamadani and his several pupils, giving the point its plurality of teachers; the Mulla ʿAbd al-Samad disambiguation is a side remark within it.

¶16.label: advance
¶16.why: Supplies the 'none in a Sufi order' half of the point with Tabatabaʾi's own words.

¶17.label: advance
¶17.why: Supplies 'of this road': the named teachers taught knowledge of the self, the method the book describes.

¶18.label: advance
¶18.why: Why a test is needed and the first exclusion: learning cannot show a teacher has walked the road.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: Second exclusion: wonders prove nothing, with Tabatabaʾi's list and reason.

¶20.label: advance
¶20.why: First positive test: the law, via Kubra's rule.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Second positive test: long company, with Tabatabaʾi's words and a pointer to the Maliki Tabrizi box.

¶22.label: advance
¶22.why: Extends the law test to the case where company is impossible: weigh the teacher's prescriptions against Book, Sunnah and Imams. A modest step, but ¶20 covered only the teacher's own conduct.

¶23.label: restate
¶23.why: That the road has pretenders and so a guide must be tested was already the premise of ¶18; the couplet and the merchandise image add colour, not a step. ¶24's 'such pretenders' could attach to ¶18 directly.

¶24.label: advance
¶24.why: Third positive test: a false guide draws people to himself, a true one turns them to God.

¶25.label: support
¶25.why: Lead-in to the ʿIsa saying that ¶26 uses; it exists only to frame the quotation.

¶26.label: support
¶26.why: Gives the ¶24 test its simplest, checkable form through ʿIsa's three marks; it does not add a new criterion but shows how any believer can apply the one already given.

¶27.label: restate
¶27.why: A summary of all five sections; every claim in it has been stated already, and the point was already reached at the end of ¶26.

¶28.label: aside
¶28.why: A bridging question to the next chapter; raises a question this chapter does not answer and the argument does not use it.
